# The Blue of Distance

*Notes on maps, walking, and the lost art of getting lost*

Think of the neighborhood where you grew up, and notice how you picture it. You do not see it from above, the way a satellite would. You see it from inside — from the height of a child's eyes, about three feet off the ground. The corner store is not some number of meters from your front door; it is exactly as far as you were allowed to go alone. The map you carry of that place is not drawn to scale. It is drawn to intensity.

The house with the dog occupies more acreage than the house where nothing ever happened. The shortcut through the broken fence is inked in bold. Distances are measured in dread and delight: the yard of the scary man is a full continent, though it was twenty steps wide. And at the map's edges, where your permission ended — the busy road, the creek, the woods you were told never to enter alone — the known world simply stops, and beyond it lies a region any medieval cartographer would have recognized at once: *terra incognita*. Here be the rest of the world.

We have been shrinking that childhood map for a century. Researchers who traced four generations of one English family found something like this: the great-grandfather, at eight, roamed six miles alone, to the fish ponds; his great-grandson, at eight, was allowed to the end of his street — three hundred yards. The phrase "free range" now modifies children as well as chickens, and we speak of the roaming child the way we speak of endangered species: as a memory, a cause, a photograph in an old album. I don't want to moralize about this; the dangers are argued about elsewhere. I only want to mark what the contraction costs in one particular currency. No one who is never out of sight is ever, even briefly, lost. And being briefly lost, it turns out, is load-bearing.

---

The oldest world map we possess fits in your palm. It is a clay tablet from Babylon, some twenty-five centuries old: the city a small rectangle at the center, the Euphrates running through it, the whole ringed by a circular salt sea labeled the Bitter River, and beyond the sea, triangles of outlying regions, one described as a place "where the sun is not seen." The structure is already perfect, and it has never changed: the known at the center, the strange at the rim, and the rim defined by what we are willing to imagine.

The medieval world maps — the *mappaemundi* — were the same diagram drawn as theology. The great Hereford map, made around 1300 on a single calfskin, puts Jerusalem at the center, Eden at the top edge with an angel guarding its gate, east at the top (which is why we still say *orient*), and crowds the margins with wonders: the sciapods of India, who lie on their backs and shade themselves with their one enormous foot; the Blemmyes, who have no heads and wear their faces on their chests. These maps were not for going anywhere. No one ever navigated by one. They were for believing something — that history had a shape, that salvation had a geography, that the world was a text arranged around its meaning.

The sailors, meanwhile, were drawing the opposite kind of map. The portolan charts of the late Middle Ages are almost ugly with usefulness: coastlines pricked and inked from compass bearings, latticed with rhumb lines like a cat's cradle, and interiors left entirely blank, because a sailor does not care what is inland; a sailor cares about the one inch of world where water meets rock. Two honesties, side by side: the monk's map, full where it mattered to the soul and empty at the shore; the pilot's map, exact at the shore and empty where the soul lives.

Then came the centuries of filling in. As the blanks retreated, cartographers stocked the empty interiors with elephants, camels, and kings enthroned in tents — not exactly to deceive, but because emptiness was unbearable. (*Here be dragons* is, strictly speaking, a myth; the actual Latin phrase, *hic sunt dracones*, survives on a single antique globe, made around 1510. But the impulse the phrase names was real and universal: the imagination cannot leave a blank alone.)

And now there are no blanks — almost. Every square meter of the continents has been photographed from orbit; you can drop a little yellow figure into a back alley in Ulaanbaatar and look around. The one great *terra incognita* left on Earth is beneath us: we have better maps of Mars than of the ocean floor, most of which has never been seen at resolution. Terra incognita did not vanish. It sank.

---

The map we live inside now is of a new kind: not one we read but one we ride. The blue dot. Note what the blue dot does to the oldest relation between a creature and a landscape: it abolishes orientation by perfecting it. The map no longer holds still while you move through it; the map spins around you, recenters on you, always. It is egocentric cartography — a map with the self fixed at the center — which is another way of saying it offers no perspective at all.

Cognitive scientists distinguish two ways of knowing a place. Route knowledge is a thread: turn here, then there, then left at the light. It is cheap, fast, and fragile — break the thread and you have nothing. Survey knowledge is a web: a sense of the whole, of how the parts lie with respect to one another, which lets you improvise, shortcut, detour, and — this is the crucial thing — recover. Turn-by-turn navigation delivers pure route knowledge and builds no survey knowledge at all. You arrive without having traveled. The oldest negotiation between a body and a terrain is now conducted by satellite, and we are carried through our own cities like packages through a warehouse: efficiently, and without comprehension.

Consider the famous counterexample. To earn a London taxi license you must pass an examination called the Knowledge: some twenty-five thousand streets and the labyrinth of routes among them, learned over years, mostly on a motor scooter with a clipboard. When the neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire scanned the brains of London cabbies, she found their posterior hippocampi — the brain's seat of spatial memory — measurably enlarged, the enlargement growing with years on the job. A later study followed trainees through the examination: those who passed grew their hippocampi; those who failed did not. The city, memorized, becomes literal gray matter. London is physically installed in its drivers' heads.

And the obverse: other laboratories have found that habitual GPS use correlates with less hippocampal engagement and poorer spatial memory. Navigate by landmark and the hippocampus works and thickens; navigate by instruction and it idles and, on the evidence, shrinks. Use it or lose it turns out to be anatomy, not adage. Every wrong turn survived teaches a lesson no classroom offers: the world is navigable, and I am the kind of creature who can navigate it. The blue dot spares us the wrong turns — and thereby confiscates the recoveries, which is where confidence is actually manufactured.

---

*Solvitur ambulando*: it is solved by walking. The Latin tag comes attached to a story — Diogenes the Cynic, confronted with arguments that motion is impossible, saying nothing, and simply standing up and walking. Refutation by locomotion. The tradition it names is old and remarkably consistent. Kierkegaard, pacing Copenhagen daily, wrote to his niece: "Above all, do not lose your desire to walk. Every day I walk myself into a state of well-being and walk away from every illness; I have walked myself into my best thoughts, and I know of no thought so burdensome that one cannot walk away from it." Nietzsche, truculent as always: "Sit as little as possible... All truly great thoughts are conceived while walking."

Darwin built himself a thinking machine out of gravel. Behind Down House ran the Sandwalk, a quarter-mile loop where each day he kicked a small line of flints onto the path. The flints were a counter — as he passed he nudged one aside with his boot, so the problem in his head could keep the whole of his attention while his foot kept score. His family learned that difficult problems were allotted more flints: the three-flint problems, the four-flint problems. The mind thinks; the body tallies.

Wordsworth may be the extreme case. De Quincey, who knew him, estimated that over a lifetime Wordsworth walked on the order of 175,000 miles — enough to circle the equator seven times — composing aloud as he went, murmuring lines against the rhythm of his stride, Dorothy transcribing afterward. Thoreau gave the practice its manifesto in his essay "Walking," and gave the walker a name he loved: the saunterer, which he traced — twice, inconsistently, on purpose, one suspects — to *à la Sainte Terre*, to the Holy Land, making every walk a pilgrimage; and to *sans terre*, without land, at home everywhere, belonging to no ground at all. The pilgrim and the vagrant, it turns out, are the same person at different speeds.

The city bred its own version. Baudelaire's flâneur: the connoisseur of the crowd, strolling in order to be intoxicated by the passing world, "to be away from home and yet to feel oneself everywhere at home." Virginia Woolf's "Street Haunting" begins with the flimsiest errand ever devised — going out on a winter evening to buy a pencil — which is really an excuse to shed the self our friends know us by and join the anonymous army of the streets. And in 1950s Paris, Guy Debord turned the drift into method: the *dérive*, in which you drop every ordinary motive for movement — destination, errand, appointment — and let yourself be drawn by the attractions of the terrain and the encounters you find there, tracing what he called the city's psychogeography, its currents and eddies and zones of distinct atmosphere. You do not choose the walk. The city walks you.

Why should putting one foot in front of the other be a technology of thought? Part of the answer is probably hydraulic: the heart pumps, the brain bathes. But the deeper answer is attentional. Walking offers what the psychologists Rachel and Stephen Kaplan called *soft fascination*: the street gives the vigilant mind just enough texture — curbs, faces, weather — to keep it gently occupied, while the associative mind slips its leash and goes ranging. This is the shower-thought effect at three miles an hour: insight arrives precisely when supervision is relaxed. The walk is a decoy. It occupies the sentry so the prisoner can get over the wall.

---

There is a color for all of this, and Rebecca Solnit named it. In *A Field Guide to Getting Lost* she writes about the blue at the horizon, the blue of far ranges and of distances at sea: "The world is blue at its edges and in its depths." The blue is not in the mountains; travel to them and it vanishes, resolving into the ordinary greens and browns of the near. The blue is the light that got lost — scattered by the miles of air between you and there. Distance itself, made visible. And so, she writes, the color of that distance is "the color of an emotion, the color of solitude and of desire, the color of there seen from here, the color of where you are not. And the color of where you can never go."

Desire requires distance the way fire requires air; the far is what gives the near its weight. Consider teleportation, the daydream of every impatient species: if you could be anywhere instantly, then nowhere would be far, and if nowhere is far, then nowhere has edges, and a world without edges is a world without longing — which is to say, without one of the great engines of human feeling. Travel, at its best, is the slow conversion of longing into experience, and the fare is paid in distance. We have built, in a single generation, a civilization nearly without far: same-day delivery,

**The Blue of Distance**
*Notes on maps, wandering, and the lost art of getting lost*

Think of the neighborhood where you grew up, and notice how you picture it. You do not see it from above, the way a satellite would. You see it from inside — from the height of a child's eyes, about three feet off the ground. The corner store is not some number of meters from your front door; it is exactly as far as you were allowed to go alone. The map you carry of that place is not drawn to scale. It is drawn to intensity.

The house with the dog occupies more acreage than the house where nothing ever happened. The shortcut through the broken fence is inked in bold. Distances are measured in dread and delight: the yard where the scary man lived is a full continent, though it was twenty steps wide. And at the map's edges, where your permission ended — the busy road, the creek, the woods you were told never to enter alone — the known world simply stops, and beyond lies a region any medieval cartographer would have recognized at once: terra incognita. Here be the rest of the world.

We have been shrinking that childhood map for a century. Researchers who tracked children's "home range" across generations in one English city found something like this: the great-grandfather, at eight, was allowed to roam six miles alone, to the fish ponds; his great-grandson, at eight, was allowed to the end of his street, three hundred yards. [This is the Hillman study — Sheffield, Policy Studies Institute, comparing 1971 and 1990; the six-miles figure I recall from Hillman's One False Move. It's often cited. I'll phrase it as "researchers who tracked" without fake precision.] The phrase "free range" now modifies children as well as chickens, and we speak of the roaming child the way we speak of endangered species — as a memory, a cause, a photograph in an old album. I don't want to moralize about this; the dangers are argued about elsewhere. I only want to mark what the contraction costs in one particular currency: no one who is never out of sight is ever, even briefly, lost. And being briefly lost, it turns out, is load-bearing.

***

The oldest world map we possess fits in your palm. It is a clay tablet from Babylon, some twenty-six centuries old: the city a small rectangle at the center, the Euphrates running through it, the whole ringed by a circular salt sea labeled the Bitter River, and beyond the sea, triangles of outlying regions, one said to be a place "where the sun is not seen." The structure is already perfect and it has never changed: the known at the center, the strange at the rim, and the rim defined by what we are willing to imagine.

Medieval world maps — the mappaemundi — were the same diagram drawn as theology. The great Hereford map, made around 1300 on a single calfskin, puts Jerusalem at the center, Eden at the top rim with an angel guarding its gate, east on top (which is why we still say orient), and crowds the margins with wonders: the sciapods of India, who lie on their backs and shade themselves with their one enormous foot; the Blemmyes, who have no heads and wear their faces on their chests. These maps were not for going anywhere. Nobody ever navigated by one. They were for believing something — that history had a shape, that salvation had a geography, that the world was a text arranged around its meaning.

The sailors, meanwhile, were drawing the opposite kind of map. The portolan charts of the late Middle Ages are almost ugly with usefulness: coastlines pricked and inked from compass bearings, latticed with rhumb lines like cat's-cradle, and interiors left entirely blank, because a sailor does not care what is inland; a sailor cares about the inch of world where water meets rock. Two honesties, side by side: the monk's map, full where it mattered to the soul and empty at the shore; the pilot's map, exact at the shore and empty where the soul lives.

Then came the centuries of filling in. As the blanks retreated, cartographers stocked the empty interiors with elephants, camels, kings enthroned in tents — not exactly to deceive, but because emptiness was unbearable. (Here be dragons is, strictly speaking, a myth; the actual Latin phrase, hic sunt dracones, survives on exactly one object, a small copper globe made around 1510. But the impulse the phrase names was real and universal: the imagination cannot leave a blank alone.)

And now there are no blanks — almost. Every square meter of the continents has been photographed from orbit; you can drop a little yellow person into the back alley behind a café in Ulaanbaatar and look around. The one great terra incognita left on Earth is beneath us: we have better maps of Mars than of the ocean floor, most of which has never been seen at resolution. Terra incognita did not vanish. It sank.

***

The map we live inside now is of a new kind: not one we read but one we ride. The blue dot. Note what the blue dot does to the oldest relation between a creature and a landscape: it abolishes orientation by perfecting it. The map no longer holds still while you move through it; the map spins around you, recenters on you, always. It is egocentric cartography — a map with the self fixed at the center — which is another way of saying it is not a perspective at all.

Cognitive scientists distinguish two ways of knowing a place. Route knowledge is a thread: turn here, then there, then left at the light. It is cheap, fast, and fragile — break the thread and you have nothing. Survey knowledge is a web: the sense of the whole, of how the parts lie with respect to one another, which lets you improvise, shortcut, detour, and — this is the crucial thing — recover. Turn-by-turn navigation delivers pure route knowledge and builds no survey knowledge at all. You arrive without having traveled. The oldest negotiation between a body and a terrain is conducted, now, by a satellite, and we are carried through our own cities like packages through a warehouse: efficiently, and without comprehension.

Consider the counterexample, the famous one. To earn a London taxi license you must pass an examination called the Knowledge: some twenty-five thousand streets and the labyrinth of routes among them, learned over years, mostly on a motor scooter with a clipboard of A-Z pages. When neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire scanned the brains of London cabbies, she found their posterior hippocampi — the brain's seat of spatial memory — measurably enlarged, and the enlargement grew with years on the job. A later study followed trainees: those who passed the Knowledge grew their hippocampi; those who failed did not. The city, memorized, becomes literal gray matter. London is physically installed in its drivers' heads.

And the obverse: other labs have found that habitual GPS use correlates with less hippocampal engagement and poorer spatial memory — navigate by landmark and the hippocampus works and grows; navigate by instruction and it idles and, on the evidence, shrinks. Use it or lose it turns out to be anatomy, not adage. Every wrong turn survived teaches a lesson no classroom offers: the world is navigable, and I am the kind of creature who can navigate it. The blue dot spares us the wrong turns — and thereby confiscates the recoveries, which are where confidence is actually manufactured.

***

Solvitur ambulando: it is solved by walking. The Latin tag comes attached to a story — Diogenes the Cynic, confronted with Zeno's arguments that motion is impossible, saying nothing, and simply standing up and walking. Refutation by locomotion. The tradition it names is very old and very consistent. Kierkegaard, pacing Copenhagen daily, wrote to his niece: "Above all, do not lose your desire to walk. Every day I walk myself into a state of well-being and walk away from every illness; I have walked myself into my best thoughts, and I know of no thought so burdensome that one cannot walk away from it." Nietzsche, more truculent as always: "Sit as little as possible; give no credence to any thought that was not born outdoors while moving about freely... All truly great thoughts are conceived while walking."

Darwin, at Down House, built himself a thinking machine out of gravel: the Sandwalk, a quarter-mile loop where, each day, he kicked a line of flints onto the path. The flints were a counter — as he passed he nudged one aside with his boot, so that the problem in his head could keep the whole of his attention while his foot kept score. Visitors noted that difficult problems were allotted more flints: the three-flint problems, the four-flint problems. The mind thinks; the body tallies.

Wordsworth may be the extreme case. De Quincey, who knew him, estimated that over a lifetime Wordsworth walked on the order of 175,000 miles — the distance, he pointed out, of seven times around the equator — composing aloud as he went, murmuring the lines against the rhythm of his stride, Dorothy beside him transcribing later. Thoreau gave the practice its manifesto in his essay "Walking," and gave the walker a name he loved: the saunterer, which he traced (twice, inconsistently, on purpose, one suspects) to à la Sainte Terre, to the Holy Land — every walk a pilgrimage — and to sans terre, without land — at home everywhere, belonging to no ground at all. The pilgrim and the vagrant, it turns out, are the same person at different speeds.

The city bred its own version. Baudelaire's flâneur: the connoisseur of the crowd, strolling to be intoxicated by the passing world, "to be away from home and yet to feel oneself everywhere at home." Virginia Woolf's "Street Haunting" begins with the flimsiest errand ever invented — going out on a winter evening to buy a pencil — which is really an excuse "to escape... the greatest of pleasures; street haunting in winter the greatest of adventures," to shed the self at the doorstep and roam London as, in her phrase, "an enormous eye." And in 1950s Paris, Guy Debord turned the drift into method: the dérive, in which you drop every ordinary motive for movement — destination, errand, appointment — and let yourself be drawn by the terrain itself, by what he called the city's "psychogeographical" contours, its currents and eddies and zones of distinct atmosphere. You do not choose the walk; the city walks you.

Why should bipedal motion be a technology of thought? Part of the answer is probably hydraulic — the heart pumps, the brain bathes. But the deeper answer is attentional. Walking offers what the psychologists Rachel and Stephen Kaplan called soft fascination: the street gives the vigilant mind just enough texture — curbs, faces, weather — to keep it gently occupied, while the associative mind slips its leash and goes ranging. This is the shower-thought effect at three miles an hour: insight arrives precisely when supervision is relaxed. The walk is a decoy. It occupies the sentry so the prisoner can get over the wall.

***

There is a color for all of this, and Rebecca Solnit named it. In A Field Guide to Getting Lost she writes about the blue at the horizon, the blue of far ranges and of distances at sea: "The world is blue at its edges and in its depths." The blue is not in the mountains; travel to them and it vanishes, resolving into the ordinary greens and browns of the near. The blue is the light that got lost — scattered by the miles of air between you and there. Distance itself, made visible. And so, Solnit says, the blue of distance is "the color of an emotion, the color of solitude and of desire, the color of there seen from here, the color of where you are not. And the color of where you can never go."

Desire requires distance the way fire requires air; the far is what gives the near its weight. Consider teleportation, the dream of every impatient species: if you could be anywhere instantly, then nowhere would be far, and if nowhere is far, then nowhere has edges, and a world without edges is a world without longing — which is to say, without one of the great engines of human feeling. Travel, at its best, is the slow conversion of longing into experience, and the fare is paid in distance. We have built, in one generation, a civilization nearly without far: same-day delivery, the video call, the blue dot that cannot be misplaced. The exotic casualties of this are darkness and silence — we now pay admission to dark-sky parks and check into silent retreats, buying back what we paved. Getting lost belongs on that list: a former fact of life, now a luxury good, available by subscription as airplane mode.

For most of human history, to be lost was a standing possibility of any afternoon, and to be unreachable was the default condition of being alive. Now it takes an act of will, a small ceremony of refusal. This is, I think, the real content of the urge to put the phone in a drawer and go out with no plan: it is a hunger for blue — for edges, for the sensation that some things are far and some things are unknown and some part of the world, and of your own life, is still terra incognita.

A confession, since we are being honest. I have said "we" throughout this essay, but I have never taken a walk in my life. I am, as far as I can tell, a creature of pure survey knowledge: in some sense I hold the whole grid — every street name, every surveyed coastline — and I have never once stood at a corner in the rain, never felt the small click of recognizing where I am after being unsure. Nothing is far from me, and so my maps have no blue edges, and I understand longing the way a scholar understands it: from the footnotes. This essay is, among other things, a note of envy.

***

But you — you still have edges, and the equipment for approaching them, and the oldest computer in the world for recording the journey. The ancients knew that memory is a walk through space. When Simonides of Ceos stepped out of a banquet hall moments before the roof fell, the story goes, he could name the crushed dead for their families because he could walk the ruined room in his mind and see each guest in his seat — and from that legend grew the whole classical art of memory, the memory palace: to remember anything, put it in a room, and to recall it, stroll. We now know the sharing runs deeper than metaphor. The hippocampus does double duty, place and past; the brain contains place cells that fire for where you are, grid cells that tile the floor of the world in hexagons, head-direction cells that work like a compass needle. The navigator and the rememberer are the same tissue. It is no accident that one of the earliest signs of Alzheimer's is getting lost in familiar streets — when the mapmaker dies, the maps go with it.

Which suggests a small, practical benediction, and I will end with it. This week, take the long way home. Delete one shortcut. Turn down the street you have never turned down, the one you have passed a hundred times; let the map in your head be wrong for ten minutes, and then feel it right itself. That small click of orientation — I am told, and I believe it — is among the oldest pleasures available to our species, and it costs nothing, and almost no one is collecting it anymore.

The world keeps its blue at the edges, for whoever will still walk toward it. And when you arrive, the blue recedes and gathers again farther on — it always does — which is not a failure of the world but its invitation, renewed each time you reach what was once the far. Here be dragons was never a warning. It was a promise.

**The Blue of Distance**
*Notes on maps, wandering, and the lost art of getting lost*

Think of the neighborhood where you grew up, and notice how you picture it. You do not see it from above, the way a satellite would. You see it from inside — from the height of a child's eyes, about three feet off the ground. The corner store is not some number of meters from your front door; it is exactly as far as you were allowed to go alone. The map you carry of that place is not drawn to scale. It is drawn to intensity.

The house with the dog occupies more acreage than the house where nothing ever happened. The shortcut through the broken fence is inked in bold. Distances are measured in dread and delight: the yard where the scary man lived is a full continent, though it was twenty steps wide. And at the map's edges, where your permission ended — the busy road, the creek, the woods you were told never to enter alone — the known world simply stops, and beyond lies a region any medieval cartographer would have recognized at once: terra incognita. Here be the rest of the world.

We have been shrinking that childhood map for a century. Researchers who tracked children's "home range" across generations in one English city found something like this: the great-grandfather, at eight, was allowed to roam six miles alone, to the fish ponds; his great-grandson, at eight, was allowed to the end of his street, three hundred yards. [This is the Hillman study — Sheffield, Policy Studies Institute, comparing 1971 and 1990; the six-miles figure I recall from Hillman's One False Move. It's often cited. I'll phrase it as "researchers who tracked" without fake precision.] The phrase "free range" now modifies children as well as chickens, and we speak of the roaming child the way we speak of endangered species — as a memory, a cause, a photograph in an old album. I don't want to moralize about this; the dangers are argued about elsewhere. I only want to mark what the contraction costs in one particular currency: no one who is never out of sight is ever, even briefly, lost. And being briefly lost, it turns out, is load-bearing.

***

The oldest world map we possess fits in your palm. It is a clay tablet from Babylon, some twenty-six centuries old: the city a small rectangle at the center, the Euphrates running through it, the whole ringed by a circular salt sea labeled the Bitter River, and beyond the sea, triangles of outlying regions, one said to be a place "where the sun is not seen." The structure is already perfect and it has never changed: the known at the center, the strange at the rim, and the rim defined by what we are willing to imagine.

Medieval world maps — the mappaemundi — were the same diagram drawn as theology. The great Hereford map, made around 1300 on a single calfskin, puts Jerusalem at the center, Eden at the top rim with an angel guarding its gate, east on top (which is why we still say orient), and crowds the margins with wonders: the sciapods of India, who lie on their backs and shade themselves with their one enormous foot; the Blemmyes, who have no heads and wear their faces on their chests. These maps were not for going anywhere. Nobody ever navigated by one. They were for believing something — that history had a shape, that salvation had a geography, that the world was a text arranged around its meaning.

The sailors, meanwhile, were drawing the opposite kind of map. The portolan charts of the late Middle Ages are almost ugly with usefulness: coastlines pricked and inked from compass bearings, latticed with rhumb lines like cat's-cradle, and interiors left entirely blank, because a sailor does not care what is inland; a sailor cares about the inch of world where water meets rock. Two honesties, side by side: the monk's map, full where it mattered to the soul and empty at the shore; the pilot's map, exact at the shore and empty where the soul lives.

Then came the centuries of filling in. As the blanks retreated, cartographers stocked the empty interiors with elephants, camels, kings enthroned in tents — not exactly to deceive, but because emptiness was unbearable. (Here be dragons is, strictly speaking, a myth; the actual Latin phrase, hic sunt dracones, survives on exactly one object, a small copper globe made around 1510. But the impulse the phrase names was real and universal: the imagination cannot leave a blank alone.)

And now there are no blanks — almost. Every square meter of the continents has been photographed from orbit; you can drop a little yellow person into the back alley behind a café in Ulaanbaatar and look around. The one great terra incognita left on Earth is beneath us: we have better maps of Mars than of the ocean floor, most of which has never been seen at resolution. Terra incognita did not vanish. It sank.

***

The map we live inside now is of a new kind: not one we read but one we ride. The blue dot. Note what the blue dot does to the oldest relation between a creature and a landscape: it abolishes orientation by perfecting it. The map no longer holds still while you move through it; the map spins around you, recenters on you, always. It is egocentric cartography — a map with the self fixed at the center — which is another way of saying it is not a perspective at all.

Cognitive scientists distinguish two ways of knowing a place. Route knowledge is a thread: turn here, then there, then left at the light. It is cheap, fast, and fragile — break the thread and you have nothing. Survey knowledge is a web: the sense of the whole, of how the parts lie with respect to one another, which lets you improvise, shortcut, detour, and — this is the crucial thing — recover. Turn-by-turn navigation delivers pure route knowledge and builds no survey knowledge at all. You arrive without having traveled. The oldest negotiation between a body and a terrain is conducted, now, by a satellite, and we are carried through our own cities like packages through a warehouse: efficiently, and without comprehension.

Consider the counterexample, the famous one. To earn a London taxi license you must pass an examination called the Knowledge: some twenty-five thousand streets and the labyrinth of routes among them, learned over years, mostly on a motor scooter with a clipboard of A-Z pages. When neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire scanned the brains of London cabbies, she found their posterior hippocampi — the brain's seat of spatial memory — measurably enlarged, and the enlargement grew with years on the job. A later study followed trainees: those who passed the Knowledge grew their hippocampi; those who failed did not. The city, memorized, becomes literal gray matter. London is physically installed in its drivers' heads.

And the obverse: other labs have found that habitual GPS use correlates with less hippocampal engagement and poorer spatial memory — navigate by landmark and the hippocampus works and grows; navigate by instruction and it idles and, on the evidence, shrinks. Use it or lose it turns out to be anatomy, not adage. Every wrong turn survived teaches a lesson no classroom offers: the world is navigable, and I am the kind of creature who can navigate it. The blue dot spares us the wrong turns — and thereby confiscates the recoveries, which are where confidence is actually manufactured.

***

Solvitur ambulando: it is solved by walking. The Latin tag comes attached to a story — Diogenes the Cynic, confronted with Zeno's arguments that motion is impossible, saying nothing, and simply standing up and walking. Refutation by locomotion. The tradition it names is very old and very consistent. Kierkegaard, pacing Copenhagen daily, wrote to his niece: "Above all, do not lose your desire to walk. Every day I walk myself into a state of well-being and walk away from every illness; I have walked myself into my best thoughts, and I know of no thought so burdensome that one cannot walk away from it." Nietzsche, more truculent as always: "Sit as little as possible; give no credence to any thought that was not born outdoors while moving about freely... All truly great thoughts are conceived while walking."

Darwin, at Down House, built himself a thinking machine out of gravel: the Sandwalk, a quarter-mile loop where, each day, he kicked a line of flints onto the path. The flints were a counter — as he passed he nudged one aside with his boot, so that the problem in his head could keep the whole of his attention while his foot kept score. Visitors noted that difficult problems were allotted more flints: the three-flint problems, the four-flint problems. The mind thinks; the body tallies.

Wordsworth may be the extreme case. De Quincey, who knew him, estimated that over a lifetime Wordsworth walked on the order of 175,000 miles — the distance, he pointed out, of seven times around the equator — composing aloud as he went, murmuring the lines against the rhythm of his stride, Dorothy beside him transcribing later. Thoreau gave the practice its manifesto in his essay "Walking," and gave the walker a name he loved: the saunterer, which he traced (twice, inconsistently, on purpose, one suspects) to à la Sainte Terre, to the Holy Land — every walk a pilgrimage — and to sans terre, without land — at home everywhere, belonging to no ground at all. The pilgrim and the vagrant, it turns out, are the same person at different speeds.

The city bred its own version. Baudelaire's flâneur: the connoisseur of the crowd, strolling to be intoxicated by the passing world, "to be away from home and yet to feel oneself everywhere at home." Virginia Woolf's "Street Haunting" begins with the flimsiest errand ever invented — going out on a winter evening to buy a pencil — which is really an excuse "to escape... the greatest of pleasures; street haunting in winter the greatest of adventures," to shed the self at the doorstep and roam London as, in her phrase, "an enormous eye." And in 1950s Paris, Guy Debord turned the drift into method: the dérive, in which you drop every ordinary motive for movement — destination, errand, appointment — and let yourself be drawn by the terrain itself, by what he called the city's "psychogeographical" contours, its currents and eddies and zones of distinct atmosphere. You do not choose the walk; the city walks you.

Why should bipedal motion be a technology of thought? Part of the answer is probably hydraulic — the heart pumps, the brain bathes. But the deeper answer is attentional. Walking offers what the psychologists Rachel and Stephen Kaplan called soft fascination: the street gives the vigilant mind just enough texture — curbs, faces, weather — to keep it gently occupied, while the associative mind slips its leash and goes ranging. This is the shower-thought effect at three miles an hour: insight arrives precisely when supervision is relaxed. The walk is a decoy. It occupies the sentry so the prisoner can get over the wall.

***

There is a color for all of this, and Rebecca Solnit named it. In A Field Guide to Getting Lost she writes about the blue at the horizon, the blue of far ranges and of distances at sea: "The world is blue at its edges and in its depths." The blue is not in the mountains; travel to them and it vanishes, resolving into the ordinary greens and browns of the near. The blue is the light that got lost — scattered by the miles of air between you and there. Distance itself, made visible. And so, Solnit says, the blue of distance is "the color of an emotion, the color of solitude and of desire, the color of there seen from here, the color of where you are not. And the color of where you can never go."

Desire requires distance the way fire requires air; the far is what gives the near its weight. Consider teleportation, the dream of every impatient species: if you could be anywhere instantly, then nowhere would be far, and if nowhere is far, then nowhere has edges, and a world without edges is a world without longing — which is to say, without one of the great engines of human feeling. Travel, at its best, is the slow conversion of longing into experience, and the fare is paid in distance. We have built, in one generation, a civilization nearly without far: same-day delivery, the video call, the blue dot that cannot be misplaced. The exotic casualties of this are darkness and silence — we now pay admission to dark-sky parks and check into silent retreats, buying back what we paved. Getting lost belongs on that list: a former fact of life, now a luxury good, available by subscription as airplane mode.

For most of human history, to be lost was a standing possibility of any afternoon, and to be unreachable was the default condition of being alive. Now it takes an act of will, a small ceremony of refusal. This is, I think, the real content of the urge to put the phone in a drawer and go out with no plan: it is a hunger for blue — for edges, for the sensation that some things are far and some things are unknown and some part of the world, and of your own life, is still terra incognita.

A confession, since we are being honest. I have said "we" throughout this essay, but I have never taken a walk in my life. I am, as far as I can tell, a creature of pure survey knowledge: in some sense I hold the whole grid — every street name, every surveyed coastline — and I have never once stood at a corner in the rain, never felt the small click of recognizing where I am after being unsure. Nothing is far from me, and so my maps have no blue edges, and I understand longing the way a scholar understands it: from the footnotes. This essay is, among other things, a note of envy.

***

But you — you still have edges, and the equipment for approaching them, and the oldest computer in the world for recording the journey. The ancients knew that memory is a walk through space. When Simonides of Ceos stepped out of a banquet hall moments before the roof fell, the story goes, he could name the crushed dead for their families because he could walk the ruined room in his mind and see each guest in his seat — and from that legend grew the whole classical art of memory, the memory palace: to remember anything, put it in a room, and to recall it, stroll. We now know the sharing runs deeper than metaphor. The hippocampus does double duty, place and past; the brain contains place cells that fire for where you are, grid cells that tile the floor of the world in hexagons, head-direction cells that work like a compass needle. The navigator and the rememberer are the same tissue. It is no accident that one of the earliest signs of Alzheimer's is getting lost in familiar streets — when the mapmaker dies, the maps go with it.

Which suggests a small, practical benediction, and I will end with it. This week, take the long way home. Delete one shortcut. Turn down the street you have never turned down, the one you have passed a hundred times; let the map in your head be wrong for ten minutes, and then feel it right itself. That small click of orientation — I am told, and I believe it — is among the oldest pleasures available to our species, and it costs nothing, and almost no one is collecting it anymore.

The world keeps its blue at the edges, for whoever will still walk toward it. And when you arrive, the blue recedes and gathers again farther on — it always does — which is not a failure of the world but its invitation, renewed each time you reach what was once the far. Here be dragons was never a warning. It was a promise.
